questions.prompt: What central failure is Grove trying to correct in this chapter?
choices: Organizations that value expertise but tolerate weak execution
Companies that lack enough creative ideas
Teams that avoid ambitious language

explanation.gentle: The chapter starts with a gap between smart thinking and reliable delivery. Grove matters because he wanted goals to close that gap.
explanation.direct: The core tension is expertise without disciplined execution. OKRs are presented as a response to that management failure.
explanation.competitive: Grove was not fixing low intelligence. He was fixing intelligence that kept excusing soft follow-through.

questions.prompt: Why does the chapter call Andy Grove the father of OKRs?
choices: Because he marketed the acronym more aggressively than anyone else
Because he built the method as a discipline for clarity, ownership, and proof
Because he used OKRs only after John Doerr introduced them

explanation.gentle: Nice catch. The chapter ties Grove to the method's deeper managerial logic, not just to its label.
explanation.direct: He matters as the builder of the discipline behind the system. The point is rigor, not branding.
explanation.competitive: Father of OKRs means source of the pressure, not source of the marketing.

questions.prompt: What does ownership add to a goal according to the chapter?
choices: It makes the goal feel more collaborative even if nobody is accountable
It turns general agreement into a burden someone can be judged on
It removes the need for measurable proof

explanation.gentle: Ownership makes the goal heavier in a useful way. Someone now carries the movement instead of merely approving it.
explanation.direct: The chapter treats ownership as the difference between shared support and visible responsibility.
explanation.competitive: Without ownership, the goal can still hide behind applause.

questions.prompt: Naomi's team has excellent ideas but keeps missing deadlines because nobody clearly owns the surviving priorities. What move best fits Grove's logic?
choices: Keep the ideas broad so nobody feels boxed in
Assign one visible owner and one proof line to each remaining priority
Add another brainstorming session before assigning responsibility

explanation.gentle: The chapter would tighten the work into owned commitments rather than ask for more discussion.
explanation.direct: Option B matches the method: choose the work, fix ownership, and define evidence before the next meeting hides the softness again.
explanation.competitive: A smart room does not need more brainstorming when the burden is still floating.

questions.prompt: Tessa's lab team can explain exactly what should happen, but no one can say who owned the missed calibration work. What chapter failure mode does this reveal?
choices: The team had too much measurable proof
The team confused understanding with execution discipline
The team should have avoided setting any priorities

explanation.gentle: The team knew the right ideas but lacked the owned structure that would turn those ideas into delivery.
explanation.direct: This is the expertise-versus-execution gap in action. Shared understanding did not become owned follow-through.
explanation.competitive: Brains were present. Burden was missing. Grove would call that a design failure.

questions.prompt: Someone says Grove's lesson is simply to be harsher with people. Why is that a weak reading of the chapter?
choices: Because the chapter says discipline is mainly about inspiration
Because the chapter is about structural rigor around choice, ownership, and proof, not abstract toughness
Because the chapter avoids discussing execution altogether

explanation.gentle: The chapter is not praising severity for its own sake. It is praising a system that makes work clearer and more answerable.
explanation.direct: Harshness is the shallow reading. Grove's actual contribution is structural discipline that reduces blur.
explanation.competitive: If you keep the tone and lose the structure, you copied the mood and missed the method.

questions.prompt: Elias rolls out OKR language at his company, but every old priority stays alive and the metrics are chosen for presentation convenience. What does the chapter call this pattern?
choices: A healthy first draft of rigor
A sign that the company values ownership too strongly
The form of rigor surviving after the force of rigor is gone

explanation.gentle: The chapter keeps this boundary visible. The language may look disciplined while the real managerial demand has been softened away.
explanation.direct: This is imitation rather than rigor. The shell remains, but choice, ownership, and proof no longer create pressure.
explanation.competitive: He kept Grove's vocabulary and dropped Grove's bite.

questions.prompt: Naomi worries that explicit ownership will make her seminar team feel less collaborative. Which answer fits the chapter best?
choices: Loose responsibility is safer because collaboration matters more than accountability
Ownership strengthens collaboration by preventing polite diffusion from replacing real follow-through
Ownership only belongs in corporate settings, not in school teams

explanation.gentle: The chapter does not treat ownership as the enemy of teamwork. It treats ownership as what keeps teamwork from going soft.
explanation.direct: Option B wins because responsibility clarifies contribution instead of eliminating collaboration.
explanation.competitive: Warmth without burden feels good until the deadline exposes the bluff.

questions.prompt: Two companies both use OKR language. One cuts priorities, fixes ownership, and names proof early. The other keeps the language but protects soft accountability. What separates them according to the chapter?
choices: Only the first company is preserving Grove's managerial rigor
Only the second company is staying flexible enough to innovate
There is no meaningful difference if both companies publish goals

explanation.gentle: The chapter says the difference is not in the vocabulary. It is in whether the system still creates real managerial consequence.
explanation.direct: The first company keeps the force of rigor, while the second keeps the form and loses the discipline.
explanation.competitive: One is using the method. The other is wearing its costume.

questions.prompt: Why does the chapter naturally point from Grove's discipline toward an Intel crisis case next?
choices: Because the chapter wants to leave management behind and move into biography
Because a method built for execution should show itself most clearly when pressure is real and time is short
Because Grove only used OKRs after Intel stopped facing competition

explanation.gentle: The bridge works because pressure reveals whether a discipline is real. Crisis makes the operating logic easier to see.
explanation.direct: If Grove's method is truly built for execution, the next strong test is an Intel moment where alignment has to happen fast.
explanation.competitive: Theory talks loudly. Crisis makes the system prove itself.
